title: Majestic Fork
reviewNotes: Three branches, 30 exact positions beginning after ...Rxf2 at 102 seconds. Rg2 offers a rook fork between f2/h2. Captures release promotion and Qe8+/Qf5+ queen forks. Declining with ...Rxf7 reaches the supported king approach to g7 against ...Rh8. Earlier nine-piece setup and eight-piece bishop interference remain context; discontinuous final promotion display is excluded.
transcript: Fools would resign. Wise players might make a draw, but only a true genius would be able to find the incredible win that white has in this position. It might seem like there's no way to make any progress. If we take the black pawn, black is actually going to give us this check, make the king move, pick up the pawn, and after the rook trade, come back to stop the promotion. And if we start advancing this pawn, we leave black the option to take the bishop, and even though it seems like we're about to promote, after this check, black is going to threaten a checkmate in one move, forcing the king to run. Black threatens a checkmate again, and after the king moves, rook to e2 seals the deal. The king cannot escape anymore, and if it comes back, this is a checkmate. But white has an incredible plan, starting with f7. Of course, black cannot allow the promotion, so it runs with the rook to f1. Now, making the queen would actually be a mistake. Black is going to give the rook for the queen, and then pick up this pawn, and the rook and bishop are not enough to win against the black rook and the pawn. But this is where it gets interesting. White now takes on h7, threatening to get two different queens, except that both of the promotions can be stopped after rook to h2. And now black seems simply out of the woods. There is no progress to be made. But actually, black is completely lost after the incredible and majestic bishop to f2. A move that looks like a mouse slip. We are hanging the bishop two different ways, but this is what it's called interference. We are placing the bishop in the way of the rook. So, the bishop has to be taken, or on the next move we are going to promote. Of course, if black takes this way, after we promote to a queen, now this is indeed enough to win against the two black rooks. But so what? Black can take with this rook and still stop both of the promotions. What kind of progress is this? Nothing has changed. But something has changed. We now have a new move available. The incredible and brilliant and absolutely beautiful rook to g2. Look at this construction. The three rooks stand side by side, and this, believe it or not, is a rook fork. The idea is pretty simple. If you take the rook, now this pawn is free to promote, and after you capture the other pawn, there is always going to be a fork with the queen that is going to pick up the rook and win the game. And nothing changes if you take this way. White is still going to promote. You can even give a check, but after the black rook takes, there is going to be a fork, and this is a winning position for white. But don't celebrate too soon, because black does have one last little trick, trying to take the pawn on f7. Now, after we take here, there is going to be a check, and the black rook actually stops the pawn, and there is no way to promote it. But luckily, our king has gained exactly the opposition against the black king, meaning that eventually, the white king is going to be able to kick the rook out, promote, and win this position. If you love incredible chess, follow me for more.
